abstract: An increasing number of central banks have begun disclosing reserve currency shares. This column introduces a new public database providing information on the reserve currency composition of 149 countries across 23 currencies, covering the period 1999 to 2026, which allows a granular analysis of the factors driving reserve currency composition. Liquidity, return, and safety are the determinants most frequently cited when explaining allocation decisions. While central banks rarely acknowledge it publicly, a growing body of evidence also suggests a role for geopolitical considerations and international alliances.
title: Inside central banks’ currency portfolios: New evidence from 149 countries and 23 currencies

abstract: Senders now have more ways than ever to move money across borders, yet costs remain high and vary widely across corridors. This column argues that a missing piece in explaining these high costs is the exchange rate risk borne by the intermediaries that move the currency, the money transfer operators. Across 339 remittance corridors worldwide, fees rise when the recipient country’s currency becomes more volatile, and this currency risk adds about as much to the price of a transfer as operators’ markups. Competition alone cannot lower these costs.
title: Currency risk drives remittance fees as much as markups do

abstract: Whether inflation can ease public debt burdens is an increasingly important question as debt sustainability concerns rise in the euro area. This column applies a new debt decomposition framework to assess how inflation affected debt ratios in the five largest euro area sovereign issuers over 2005–2025. It finds that inflation played a small role in reducing the public debt burden. The post-pandemic inflation surprise largely reflected imported costs, which do little to raise nominal output. Increases in longer-term inflation compensation lowered the market value of debt, but were not sufficient to offset the debt-increasing effect of earlier declines.
authors: Jef Boeckx, Leonardo Iania, Joris Wauters
title: The effects of inflation on euro area public debt

abstract: In the United States, for nuclear power to contribute meaningfully to future clean-energy portfolios, new plant construction must achieve cost competitiveness and demonstrate reduced risk of cost and schedule overruns—factors that directly influence federal and state energy policy, utility investment decisions, and public acceptance. Within this policy landscape, the structure of project delivery and the allocation of risk across participating firms are not merely technical construction considerations—they are central determinants of whether nuclear projects can satisfy the financial, regulatory, and societal criteria required for approval and long-term operation. Understanding how delivery models perform is therefore critical to shaping effective energy policy mechanisms, such as cost-recovery frameworks, loan-guarantee programs, risk-sharing incentives, and procurement standards. This study quantitatively analyzes historical U.S. nuclear construction data, focusing on cost and schedule overruns and the performance implications of how responsibilities were distributed among project participants. Predictor variables were introduced to contextualize the results within broader policy-relevant conditions, including regulatory uncertainty and project complexity. The findings indicate that contracting models involving 2 major actors (the most common of which is an Engineering, Procurement and Construction (EPC) contracting model) have historically exhibited improved performance compared to other contracting approaches. Projects where the Owner also performed EPC responsibilities, or where Owner, Engineering and Construction roles were all within separate firms, exhibited higher schedule overruns. This conclusion was present when controlling for the influence of geographic region, reactor design and construction date. From an energy policy perspective, this suggests that Project Delivery System (PDS) choices can affect the financial risk profile of nuclear development and, by extension, the policy tools required to support it. Strengthening these delivery mechanisms should be considered a priority within broader policy strategies aimed at enabling a reliable, affordable, and politically durable nuclear renaissance in the United States.
title: Relationship between project delivery system and historic nuclear power plant construction performance in the United States
